what: Chord Energy drills for oil and natural gas in the Williston Basin of North Dakota and Montana, the area known as the Bakken. It was formed by merging Oasis Petroleum and Whiting Petroleum, and later added Enerplus.
customers: Refiners and commodity traders who buy crude oil, and processors who buy natural gas and natural gas liquids. Prices are set by the market, not negotiated.
money: Bakken crude sold at prevailing benchmark prices less local differentials.
Associated gas produced alongside the oil, plus liquids stripped out at processing plants.
Marketing activity: buying and reselling third-party barrels, which carries revenue but thin margin.
moat: Concentrated acreage in one basin it knows well. Chord holds a large, contiguous position, which lets it drill longer horizontal wells from shared pads and cut cost per barrel. There is no brand or switching cost here, only the cost of getting a barrel out of the ground.
risks: The price of oil decides everything. A fall from current levels would compress cash flow quickly, as the move from $5.3B of revenue in 2024 to $4.9B in 2025 shows.
Shale wells decline fast, so a large share of cash flow must be reinvested every year merely to hold production flat.
Everything sits in one basin. A regulatory change in North Dakota, a pipeline outage or a cold-weather shut-in affects the whole company.
Bakken crude usually sells below the headline US benchmark because it has to travel far to reach refiners.
Debt is about $1.5B against $189.5M of cash.
opportunities: Free cash flow of roughly $1.4B against a $7.2B market value is a large yield, and Chord has returned much of it through buybacks and variable dividends.
The shares trade at about 8.6 times earnings and 2.6 times EV/EBITDA, low even for an oil producer.
The Enerplus merger added adjacent acreage, and overlapping land allows longer wells and shared infrastructure.
Sixteen analysts average a $183.38 target, roughly 35% above the current price.
watch: Cost per well and the oil price together. A shale producer is only as good as the cash a new well returns, so watch whether drilling and completion costs per foot keep falling while production per well holds up.
